218.title: Vayechi: crossed hands (Genesis 48:13–20)
218.hook: Jacob crosses his hands to bless the younger grandson first
218.howItsDone: On Friday night, before the Shabbat meal, many Jewish parents bless their children with hands on their heads: sons to be like Ephraim and Manasseh, daughters like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, followed by the priestly blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chesed ve'emet: true kindness, the kind that can't be repaid, like carrying Jacob home to be buried. Today, before he dies, Jacob meets two grandsons.

In plenty of families, the older one gets introduced first. Gets the bigger bedroom, the first car, the photo in the middle. The younger one learns to stand a little to the side. Now Joseph arranges his two sons in front of their grandfather for a blessing. He's careful. The older boy goes to Jacob's right hand, the hand of the stronger blessing. The younger goes to his left. Everything in order. Then the old man, nearly blind, does something with his arms.
screen: `THE OLDER ONE GOES FIRST.` → `JOSEPH ARRANGES HIS SONS.` → `THE OLD MAN'S ARMS.`

segments.voice: Jacob crosses his hands. His right hand goes onto the head of Ephraim, the younger. His left onto Manasseh, the firstborn. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "guiding his hands wittingly." On purpose. Joseph is upset. He takes his father's hand to move it: not that way, father, this one's the firstborn. And Jacob says: "I know it, my son, I know it." He doesn't stop. The younger one, he says, will be greater. But the older one, too, will become a people, and he too will be great. Then Jacob says: from now on, when the people of Israel bless their children, they'll say, "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." And they do. On Friday nights, in many Jewish homes, parents place their hands on their sons' heads and say exactly that. Daughters are blessed to be like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah. Why these two boys, and not the great patriarchs? One answer some teachers give: look at the brothers before them in Genesis. Cain and Abel, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau, Joseph and his brothers. Then two brothers blessed in reverse order, and the text records no quarrel between them. Another answer: they grew up in Egypt, in a palace, and stayed who they were. Genesis keeps choosing the younger. But in this scene, nobody loses. The younger one first, and the older one too.

219.title: Vayechi: twelve blessings (Genesis 49)
219.hook: each son receives a different blessing, fitted to who he is
219.howItsDone: Jacob's twelve sons became the twelve tribes of Israel, and images from these blessings, such as Judah's lion and Naphtali's deer, still appear on synagogue windows, Torah covers and Jewish art.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayechi: Jacob crossed his hands and blessed the younger grandson first. The younger one too. Today, Jacob calls in all twelve sons.

One teacher wrote the same comment on every report card. Pleasure to have in class. Nice. Harmless. And forgettable, because it wasn't about you. Then there's the teacher who said something only you could have received: the thing that stung a little and was true, or the thing that saw a gift nobody else had noticed. You probably still remember the words. Jacob is on his deathbed, his twelve sons crowded around. And he doesn't give one blessing twelve times.
screen: `THE SAME COMMENT FOR EVERYONE.` → `THE WORDS ONLY YOU COULD GET.` → `TWELVE SONS AT THE BED.`

segments.voice: Genesis forty-nine is a long poem, one of the oldest-sounding passages in the Torah, and its Hebrew is famously hard. Jacob goes son by son, and every word is different. Judah is a young lion. Zebulun will live by the shore, a harbor for ships. Issachar is a strong donkey, bending his shoulder to work. Naphtali is a deer running free. Benjamin is a wolf. Not every word is sweet. Reuben, the firstborn, is told he's unstable as water, and he loses first place. Simeon and Levi hear their father curse their anger, the violence they did years before. Then the Torah sums it up, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "every one according to his blessing he blessed them." Each one, his own. Rashi notices the word them at the end. Even Reuben, Simeon and Levi, the ones who got hard words, were blessed. A true blessing can include the truth. Other commentators point out that the lion, the harbor, the deer are about what each son is suited for: leadership, trade, work, speed. Jacob isn't handing out prizes. He's naming who each one is, and sending him toward it. Every family, every office, every classroom has its twelve different children. The Torah's picture of a blessing isn't one warm sentence for the group chat. It's attention: looking long enough at one person to know their particular strength and their particular danger, and saying so with love.

220.title: Vayechi: not in God's place (Genesis 50:15–21)
220.hook: Joseph refuses revenge: "ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good"
220.howItsDone: When the reading of a whole book of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation says chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek; Jewish law also forbids taking revenge or bearing a grudge, from Leviticus 19:18.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayechi: twelve sons, twelve different blessings. Each one his own blessing. Today, Jacob is buried, and the brothers are suddenly afraid.

There's a particular fear that shows up after a funeral. The parent who held everyone together is gone, and old debts look different. Was my brother only being nice because Dad was watching? Joseph's brothers feel exactly that. For seventeen years in Egypt, Joseph has fed and protected them. But now their father is buried, and they think: maybe he was just waiting. Maybe now he'll pay us back for the pit and the sale. So they send him a message.
screen: `AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `MAYBE HE WAS JUST WAITING.` → `THE POWER TO PUNISH.`

segments.voice: The message says: before he died, your father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers. The Torah never shows Jacob saying any such thing. The Talmud concludes they made it up, and draws a surprising rule from it: you may soften the truth for the sake of peace. Joseph hears their words, and he cries. Then the brothers come and throw themselves down: we're your slaves. Remember the dreams, the sheaves bowing, the stars bowing? Here it is, finally, the brothers on the ground. Joseph could take it. Instead he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God?" In Hebrew, ha-tachat Elohim ani. Am I standing where God stands? Judging and punishing isn't my seat. Then: "ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." He doesn't pretend. What they did was wrong, and he names it. But he refuses to be the one who settles the account. He says he'll provide for them and their little ones, and the text says he comforted them and spoke to their hearts. With that, the book of Genesis ends. Joseph dies at a hundred and ten, still in Egypt. When a congregation finishes reading a book of the Torah, it calls out together: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another.

221.title: Shemot: these are the names (Exodus 1:1)
221.hook: the book begins by naming those who went down to Egypt
221.howItsDone: In synagogues, Shemot begins the winter stretch of Exodus readings; each Hebrew book of the Torah is named for an early word, so Genesis is Bereshit, in the beginning, and Exodus is Shemot, names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Genesis: Joseph asks, am I in the place of God? Not my place to punish. Today, a new book begins.

A new manager gets your name wrong. So does a teacher with thirty kids, and a cousin at a wedding. It's small, and it can sting anyway. Then there's the opposite: someone you met once, months ago, says your name without hesitating. That one lands. The second book of the Torah, the one about slavery and freedom, could start with a king or a plague or a burning bush. It starts with a list of names.
screen: `CALLED THE WRONG NAME.` → `REMEMBERED AFTER ONE MEETING.` → `A BOOK THAT STARTS WITH NAMES.`

segments.voice: In English this book is Exodus, from the Greek for going out. In Hebrew, like the other books of the Torah, it's named for an early word: Shemot. Names. The first verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Now these are the names of the sons of Israel, who came into Egypt with Jacob." Then the list: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, and the rest. This puzzled the rabbis. Genesis already gave the names of everyone who went down to Egypt, not long before. Why repeat it? Rashi answers with a picture. The prophet Isaiah says God brings out the stars by number and calls each one by name. The Torah counts these people again, Rashi says, the way you'd count something precious, and names them to show how dear they are. A few verses later comes a chilling line: "Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph." A ruler who doesn't know the name. That's how the slavery starts. Then two midwives refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the baby boys, and the text gives their names: Shiphrah and Puah. The king of Egypt? In the whole story, he never gets a name. He's only Pharaoh, a title. The powerful man stays anonymous, and the two brave women are remembered by name. Before the story of freedom, the book stops to say who these people were.

222.title: Shemot: the lost lamb (Exodus Rabbah 2:2)
222.hook: midrash: Moses carries a runaway lamb back, and God chooses him to shepherd a people
222.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls Moses Moshe Rabbeinu, Moses our teacher, and often calls him the faithful shepherd; midrashim like this one are taught to children and adults alike to explain what the Torah leaves unsaid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: the book of Exodus begins with names, and the midwives are remembered while Pharaoh isn't. Start with the names. Today, Moses, grown up, far from Egypt, with a flock.

How do you pick a leader? A job interview. A résumé. A vote, a speech, a debate. The big moments. The Torah tells us Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew slave, fled to the desert, married, and became a shepherd for his father-in-law, Jethro. Then one day God speaks to him from a burning bush and sends him to free a nation. The Torah doesn't say why him. The rabbis wanted to know. So they told a story about an ordinary afternoon with the sheep.
screen: `HOW DO YOU PICK A LEADER?` → `PALACE, DESERT, SHEPHERD.` → `THE TORAH DOESN'T SAY WHY.`

segments.voice: The story is a midrash, a rabbinic teaching that fills a gap in the text, from a collection called Exodus Rabbah. Moses is tending Jethro's flock in the wilderness. One little animal slips away and runs. The midrash actually says a young goat; it's often retold as a lamb. Moses goes after it. It runs and runs, until it reaches a shady spot with a pool of water, and stops to drink. And Moses, out of breath, says: I didn't know you were running because you were thirsty. You must be exhausted. He picks it up, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it all the way back to the flock. That's the whole story. No miracle, no speech. And the midrash says God saw it and said: you have compassion to lead a flock that belongs to a man. By your life, you will shepherd my flock, Israel. Notice what Moses didn't do. He didn't scold the runaway. He didn't leave it, though it was one animal out of many. He assumed the running had a reason, and the reason was need. The same midrash tells a similar story about David, the shepherd boy who became king: he let the youngest sheep eat the tender grass first. In this telling, you don't find a leader on a stage. You find one when nobody is watching, when somebody small wanders off, and someone goes after them.

223.title: Shemot: holy ground (Exodus 3:5)
223.hook: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet", for the place is holy
223.howItsDone: Before the priestly blessing in synagogue, the kohanim remove their shoes, a rule the Talmud records; on Yom Kippur and Tisha b'Av, many Jews avoid leather shoes all day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: the midrash of Moses chasing a thirsty runaway and carrying it home. Carry the lamb. Today, the same shepherd, the same flock, and a bush.

Lots of homes have a rule at the door: shoes off. Some for cleanliness, some out of respect, some because a grandmother said so. Mosques, temples and many homes around the world ask the same thing. Out of their shoes, people tend to move slower and quieter, closer to the floor. Moses is in the wilderness with Jethro's sheep, at a mountain called Horeb, on an ordinary working day. He sees a bush on fire. And when God first speaks to him, right after calling his name, the subject is his shoes.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `SLOWER, QUIETER, THE FLOOR.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: The bush is burning, but it isn't burning up: the text says it was not consumed. And Moses says to himself: I'll turn aside and look at this. That's the hinge. The next verse says when God saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him. Moses, Moses. He could have walked on; plenty of people walk past strange things. He stopped. Then comes today's line, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." In Hebrew, admat kodesh. Holy earth. And it's just desert dirt with a thorny bush on it. The rabbis asked why God would speak from a scrubby thorn bush, and not a cedar or a mountaintop. One midrash answers: to show that God is with the people in their pain, down in the thorns with them. The holiness isn't in the fancy place. It's where God shows up, and where someone stops to notice. The shoes stayed with the tradition. Tradition says the priests in the ancient Temple served barefoot. To this day, when the kohanim, the priestly families, rise to bless the congregation, they take off their shoes first. And on Yom Kippur, many Jews set aside leather shoes for the whole day. Shoes are for getting somewhere. Taking them off says: I'm not going anywhere. I'm here, and this spot, right now, is enough.

segments.voice: If you can, kick off your shoes and stand, or sit with your feet flat on the floor, and feel the ground under you: its temperature, its texture. You're not going anywhere for the next two minutes. Let this ordinary spot, this floor in this room, be the place where you stopped and turned aside.
Shemot. The portion where Moses turns aside to see a burning bush and is told: take off your shoes, this ground is holy.

224.title: Shemot: signs in the hand (Exodus 4:1–9)
224.hook: a staff becomes a serpent, a hand turns white; doubt is met gently
224.tomorrow: Shemot: why hast thou dealt ill?
224.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point to Moses's reluctance at the bush as a model of humility, and the Torah later calls him the humblest of men; his staff reappears at the plagues, the sea and the rock in the wilderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: shoes off, it's holy. This week: crossed hands, twelve blessings, Joseph refusing God's place, the end of Genesis, then names, a runaway lamb and a burning bush. Today Moses, still at the bush, says: they won't believe me.

You've been offered something big: a new job, a leadership role, a chance to speak up for people. And the voice in your head doesn't say, I can't. It says something sneakier: they won't listen to me. Who am I to them? That's exactly where Moses is. God has just told him to go back to Egypt and lead the people out. And Moses, standing in front of a burning bush, argues. Not once. Several times.
screen: `OFFERED SOMETHING BIG.` → `THEY WON'T LISTEN TO ME.` → `MOSES ARGUES WITH THE BUSH.`

segments.voice: Moses says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "But, behold, they will not believe me." You'd expect thunder. Instead, God asks a question: "What is that in thy hand?" A rod, Moses says. A shepherd's staff, the most ordinary thing he owns. Throw it down, God says. It becomes a snake, and Moses runs from it. Pick it up by the tail: it's a staff again. Then: put your hand inside your cloak. He pulls it out white, diseased, like snow. Put it back, and it comes out healed. And if they still don't believe, take water from the Nile and pour it on the ground, and it'll turn to blood. Three signs, patient as a teacher with a nervous student. The Torah doesn't punish the doubt here. It meets it. Later, when Moses asks God to send someone else, the text says God grows angry, and still gives him his brother Aaron to help. Rashi adds a sharper layer. The snake and the diseased hand were also hints: by assuming his people wouldn't believe, Moses had spoken badly of them, the way the first serpent spoke badly. So the signs reassure Moses, and gently correct him. But notice where it starts. God doesn't hand Moses a new tool. The staff that led sheep becomes the staff that will split the sea. The thing you already carry may be the thing you need.
screen: `THEY WILL NOT BELIEVE ME.` · `WHAT IS THAT IN THY HAND?` · `A STAFF, A HAND, THE NILE.` · `DOUBT MET, AND GENTLY CORRECTED.` · then, large: `THE STAFF IN YOUR HAND.`

segments.voice: Think of something you doubt you can do, and ask God's question of yourself: what is that in your hand? A skill, a friendship, a habit, a bit of experience, something you've done before. Find one small sign that you're more ready than you feel, and hold it the way Moses held the staff.
Shemot. The portion where Moses doubts, and God answers with signs, starting with the staff already in his hand.
Your line: the staff in your hand. It led sheep long before it split a sea. Day two hundred twenty-four, done.
